%% Sentence for the sweep paragraph:
\cj{Across the 100 samples the frozen preconditioner costs between
0.92 and 1.04 times the iterations of a freshly
assembled one (median 1.00), and at the largest amplitude
between 0.92 and 1.04. No sample was flagged as a resonance candidate.}

%% Correlation-length sensitivity paragraph:
\cj{Shortening the correlation length from $d/4$
to $d/10$ leaves the picture unchanged. Median frozen
counts, longer against shorter: level 1, 48 against 48; level 2, 48 against 49. The rougher field costs one additional iteration at
equal amplitude, consistent with a preconditioner that responds to the size
of the deformation rather than to its spectral content.}

%% Mesh-refinement paragraph (the lambda/20 check):
\cj{Refining from $2673$ to $7269$ degrees of freedom at the top
amplitude, with the perturbation held fixed, raises the unpreconditioned
iteration count from a median of 429 to 617
(range 603--643 over 3 fields) and leaves the frozen count
where it was: 52 against 51, ranges
50--52 and 48--55. The mesh-independence that
Calder\'on preconditioning is built for therefore survives freezing the
operator on the nominal geometry, and the advantage in iteration count grows
with refinement, from 8.4 to
11.9.}

%% Campaign paragraph:
\cj{At the top amplitude, $\varepsilon = 13.3$\,mm, 100
independent fields were drawn and solved with the frozen preconditioner. The
iteration count has median 51 and range 46--58;
every sample converged to the $10^{-8}$ tolerance.
On the 20 samples also solved with a freshly assembled preconditioner
the frozen-to-fresh ratio lies between 0.93 and 1.11
(median 1.02). No realization was discarded: admissibility
is certified in advance, so the sample is the one that was drawn.}
